newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria minister says govt stalling on resignation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria minister says govt stalling on resignation.

text.p: Bulgarian Foreign Minister Georgi Pirinski, a prominent critic of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, complained on Wednesday the government was dragging its feet over accepting the resignation he offered two weeks ago.
"Normally parliament should vote my resignation, but for some reason which is not quite clear to me that is not happening," Pirinski told a news conference.
According to Bulgaria's constitution, the prime minister must introduce a minister's resignation in parliament.
Videnov is seeking to strengthen his position in the divided Socialist party ahead of a party congress next month which will discuss his critics' calls for policy changes and a cabinet shuffle.
Pirinski said he would no longer go to work in the ministry as he wanted to devote himself fully to the preparation of the December 21 and 22 congress.
Pirinski resigned on November 13, a day after the Socialists gave narrow backing to Videnov in a confidence vote.
He is often cited as a potential challenger for the prime minister's job and diplomats say Videnov's refusal to let him go weakens Pirinski's position.
Pirinski named Deputy Foreign Minister Irina Bokova as his temporary successor. He said his resignation would not affect the functioning of the ministry.
Videnov told a news conference on Tuesday he saw no urgency and was waiting for a new minister to be named so he could present Pirinski's resignation to parliament at the same time.
"According to Bulgaria's constitution, adopting of the resignation is not necesarily connected to the appointment of a new minister," Pirinski told a news conference.
The U.S.-born minister was nominated earlier this year as the Socialists' presidential candidate, but the Constitutional Court barred him from running as he was not born in Bulgaria.

The decisive defeat of the Socialists' eventual candidate, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, in the November 3 presidential run-off, widened rifts within the party and prompted fresh calls for policy reforms and a new cabinet.
